content.content:
This fictional runbook describes throttling in the Harbor microservices system and incident `SYN-EDGE-082`. All limits, service names, and observations are invented. `edge-gateway` maintains shared token buckets in Redis deployment `edge-quota-store`. That deployment is separate from the identity service's `session-store`.  
Authenticated quotas use the principal and route identifier. The default bucket refills at two requests per second, equivalent to 120 requests per minute, with capacity for a burst of twenty. Payment submission uses thirty requests per minute with burst capacity five. Token refresh uses six requests per minute with burst capacity two.

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content:
During `SYN-EDGE-082`, authenticated payment clients received HTTP 429 with `EDGE-RATE-429` after approximately six submissions per minute. Responses included `Retry-After`, expressed in seconds, and `RateLimit-Remaining=0`. Rejected requests had no matching `payments-api` trace because the gateway stopped them before forwarding.  
Payment processing latency, database acquisition time, and Kafka command age were normal for admitted requests. Several clients nevertheless displayed “Payment timed out,” making client-facing wording an unreliable guide to the response's actual origin.

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content:
A route-classifier configuration placed the broad `authenticated-write` rule ahead of the specific payment rule. The broad rule incorrectly selected bucket `auth-refresh`, applying the six-per-minute renewal quota to payment submissions. Bucket metadata and effective matcher order confirmed this mapping on every gateway replica.  
The shared quota store was reachable throughout the incident. This was a policy-selection error, not evidence that payment consumers were slow or that sessions had expired.

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content: An automated traffic surge was suggested early in the incident. Traffic volume stayed near its previous baseline, and no investigation established abusive activity. Some mobile clients may have amplified retries after receiving 429, but the available traces did not quantify that contribution.

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content:
1. Capture HTTP status, gateway reason code, route identifier, selected bucket, and `Retry-After`. Do not infer throttling solely from a client timeout message.
2. Check whether the request reached its backend. A gateway rejection should have no backend processing span for that attempt.
3. Compare the selected bucket with the route's expected refill rate and burst capacity. Shared counters mean that changing gateway replicas does not reset the allowance.
4. Distinguish HTTP 401 authentication rejection from HTTP 429 quota exhaustion. Dependency failure in `edge-quota-store` produces HTTP 503 with `EDGE-LIMIT-STORE-UNAVAILABLE` under the configured fail-closed policy.

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content:
Operators restored the specific payment matcher ahead of the broad rule and verified bucket selection with synthetic traffic. They retained the configured quotas and allowed depleted buckets to refill. Payment admission returned to normal within three minutes.  
Clients must honor `Retry-After` and add jitter when resuming requests. An explicitly rejected attempt was not admitted, but an earlier attempt may still have succeeded. Reuse the same payment idempotency key and payload when retrying the same purchase, following [payment deduplication rules](payments-idempotency.md).

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content:
Include route-to-bucket checks in configuration release validation. Alert separately on quota rejections and limiter dependency failures.  
Repeated refresh calls can exhaust the legitimate renewal bucket; use [session diagnostics](identity-session-management.md) to investigate their cause. An outage of [identity Redis](identity-redis-outage.md) affects a different store and requires different recovery actions. Follow the [escalation procedure](incident-escalation.md) for widespread checkout rejection.

metadata.title: Gateway Rate Limits and Unexpected HTTP 429 Responses

content.content:
This fictional incident record describes `SYN-ID-241` in the Harbor microservices system. All identifiers, measurements, and events are invented. On 2025-04-08, `identity-core` began signing access tokens with key identifier `sig-r32` at 09:10 UTC. Several API services continued accepting older tokens but rejected newly issued tokens for eighteen minutes.  
Access tokens are signed JWTs with an eight-minute lifetime. Services validate the issuer, audience, expiry, and signature using a cached JSON Web Key Set, abbreviated JWKS. A successful signature check does not establish that the associated user session remains active.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content:
- Protected requests returned HTTP 401 with `AUTH-JWT-013` and reason `unknown_kid`.
- Newly signed-in users failed immediately, while some existing sessions continued working until their next token refresh.
- The `jwt_unknown_key_total` counter increased only on replicas using the older JWKS cache generation.
- Session-store connectivity and token issuance latency remained normal.  
The same browser displayed a generic “Please sign in again” message for both this failure and ordinary session expiry. The response reason and validation stage were therefore more useful than the visible message.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content:
The new public key was published at the same time that signing switched to `sig-r32`. Validators used `JWKS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=3600` and did not refresh their cache when they encountered an unknown key identifier. Replicas that had fetched keys before 09:10 could not validate the new signatures.  
Responders confirmed the cause by comparing the published key identifiers with each replica's cache metadata. Both `sig-r31` and `sig-r32` were present in the published JWKS; affected replicas held only `sig-r31`. This was a key-discovery failure, not evidence that a private signing key had leaked.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content: Clock drift and an incorrect audience were considered initially. Recorded clock offsets remained below two seconds, and sampled audience values matched the configured audience. Neither hypothesis explained the selective `unknown_kid` errors. No evidence established malicious token forgery.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content:
1. Record the failing request's correlation identifier, service replica, error reason, and token `kid`. Do not copy the bearer token into incident notes.
2. Compare the `kid` with the published public-key inventory and the replica's cached inventory.
3. Check issuer, audience, `exp`, and clock offset separately. An expired token should produce `token_expired`, not `unknown_kid`.
4. If signature validation succeeds, continue with [session lifecycle diagnostics](identity-session-management.md) or the [Redis outage procedure](identity-redis-outage.md), depending on the session lookup result.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content:
Responders verified the public-key inventory and invalidated JWKS caches through the controlled cache-refresh operation. They confirmed that every replica loaded `sig-r32` before resuming the rotation schedule. Signature checks and session checks remained enabled throughout recovery.  
Synthetic sign-in, refresh, and protected-resource requests succeeded across all replicas by 09:28 UTC. The incident was marked recovered after fifteen minutes without another `AUTH-JWT-013` failure.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content:
Publish a replacement public key at least seventy minutes before activating its signer, covering the sixty-minute cache lifetime and a ten-minute margin. Retain the previous public key for at least the eight-minute token lifetime plus sixty seconds of permitted clock skew after its final issuance. Record both deadlines in the rotation checklist.  
Use the [escalation procedure](incident-escalation.md) if authentication failures become widespread. Changing session idle limits does not resolve an unknown signing key.

metadata.title: JWT Validation Failures After Signing Key Rotation

content.content:
This fictional runbook covers incident `SYN-ID-259` in the Harbor microservices system. All names, observations, and configuration revisions are synthetic. `identity-core` uses Redis deployment `session-store` for session metadata and refresh-token rotation records. Protected requests require both a valid access JWT and a successful active-session check.  
On 2025-06-11, session lookups failed even though access-token signatures remained valid. New sign-ins, token renewal, and protected account requests were affected. Public catalog browsing continued because it did not require a user session.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content:
The identity service returned HTTP 503 with `SESSION-STORE-UNAVAILABLE`. Its session lookup latency reached the 250-millisecond connection deadline, and `session_store_connect_failures_total` increased across every identity replica. One older gateway revision translated this dependency failure into a generic HTTP 401, so some users saw an inaccurate sign-in prompt.  
Redis reported normal memory use and no increase in evictions. A diagnostic workload outside the identity deployment could connect successfully. This did not prove that identity replicas had the same network access.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content:
Network policy revision `session-access-v18` allowed incoming Redis connections from workloads labeled `app=identity-edge`. Actual identity workloads carried `app=identity-core`. The policy therefore removed their access while leaving the Redis process healthy.  
Responders compared the effective policy selectors with identity workload labels. Connectivity failed from an affected identity replica and succeeded after restoring the previous policy. This evidence confirmed a network authorization error, rather than Redis memory exhaustion or expired session records.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content: A Redis leader failure and a signing-key rotation problem were suggested but unsupported by role metrics and JWT validation results. Four refresh requests lost their responses near the policy transition. Whether their rotations committed before connectivity was interrupted remained unknown until reconciliation; a connection failure alone did not establish the outcome.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content:
1. Separate signature validation from session lookup in the request trace. `unknown_kid` requires the [JWT rotation procedure](identity-jwt-validation.md), not a Redis restart.
2. Check Redis role, memory, eviction count, and connection metrics. Test connectivity from the actual identity workload context.
3. Compare workload labels, network policy revisions, and the start of connection failures. Avoid treating a successful operator diagnostic connection as universal reachability.
4. Distinguish a completed lookup returning no session from an unavailable lookup. The former can justify `session_expired`; the latter requires a dependency error.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content:
The platform responder restored `session-access-v17`, then verified connections from every identity replica. The gateway operator corrected the legacy error mapping to preserve HTTP 503 for unavailable session storage. Signature checks and active-session enforcement remained enabled.  
Responders did not restore an old Redis snapshot, because that could reintroduce revoked sessions. They inspected rotation records for the four uncertain refresh requests and required fresh sign-in where the current token family could not be established safely.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content:
Recovery required successful sign-in, refresh, protected access, and revoked-session rejection across all replicas, followed by fifteen minutes without connection failures. The policy release checklist now includes a connectivity check from the selected application identity.  
Use [session management](identity-session-management.md) for idle expiration and replay handling. The gateway's [rate-limit store](gateway-rate-limiting.md) is a separate Redis deployment; resetting its buckets cannot restore identity sessions. Follow [incident escalation](incident-escalation.md) for widespread authentication disruption.

metadata.title: Redis Unavailability During Session Validation

content.content:
This fictional runbook covers browser authentication in the Harbor microservices system and incident `SYN-ID-248`. All service names, policies, and observations are synthetic. `identity-core` issues eight-minute access JWTs and rotating refresh tokens. Session metadata resides in the Redis deployment named `session-store`.  
A session expires after thirty minutes without authenticated activity or twelve hours after sign-in, whichever comes first. Each refresh token has a seven-day expiry, but it cannot extend those session limits. A cryptographically valid access token is rejected when its referenced session has expired or been revoked.

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content:
During `SYN-ID-248`, users with several browser tabs saw intermittent sign-outs shortly after a successful refresh. Protected requests returned HTTP 401 with `AUTH-SESSION-021`; refresh requests reported `refresh_replayed`. Other users received `session_expired` after leaving a tab inactive overnight, which was expected behavior.  
The incident affected twelve percent of active synthetic browser sessions. Redis latency remained below four milliseconds, and JWT signature checks succeeded. Repeating sign-in temporarily restored access until another concurrent refresh occurred.

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content:
Two browser tabs submitted the same single-use refresh token with different `refresh_attempt_id` values. The first request rotated the token. The second looked like reuse of an already consumed credential and revoked the refresh-token family, including the current session.  
An identical retry carrying the same attempt identifier is permitted for three seconds and returns the previously recorded rotation result. That allowance did not apply because each tab generated its own identifier. Correlated rotation records confirmed this ordering; ordinary access-token expiration did not cause the family revocation.

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content: Responders initially suspected cookie loss and session-store eviction. Browser diagnostics showed the cookie was present, and Redis eviction counters did not increase. The record does not establish whether every reported sign-out shared the refresh race; four reports lacked correlation identifiers and remain unclassified.

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content:
1. Identify whether the failing operation is access validation, token renewal, or session lookup. Capture reason codes without recording cookies or refresh-token values.
2. Check the session's creation time, last authenticated activity, and revocation reason. Distinguish idle expiration from the absolute twelve-hour limit.
3. Compare rotation sequence numbers, attempt identifiers, and timestamps across tabs. A consumed token followed by family revocation supports replay detection.
4. Check for HTTP 429 responses before investigating token lifetime. A refresh loop may trigger the separate [gateway quota](gateway-rate-limiting.md).
5. If session lookup times out, follow the [Redis outage runbook](identity-redis-outage.md). A missing signing key instead requires [JWT validation diagnostics](identity-jwt-validation.md).

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content:
The browser team restored the previous release, which coordinated renewal through a single refresh owner across tabs. Transport retries retained their original attempt identifier. Responders did not disable replay detection or increase session lifetimes.  
Users whose token families were already revoked had to sign in again. Sessions that reached their idle or absolute deadline also required new authentication; refreshing the page could not revive them. After rollback, a twenty-minute multi-tab exercise completed without unintended family revocation.

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content:
Monitor `refresh_family_revoked_total` separately from expected `session_expired` responses. Exercise concurrent tabs, delayed responses, and lost refresh acknowledgments before releasing browser authentication changes. Treat an unavailable session backend as a dependency failure rather than proof that the user supplied an invalid password.  
For broad login disruption, apply the [incident severity rules](incident-escalation.md). Keep unresolved reports explicitly separate from sessions whose revocation sequence has been confirmed.

metadata.title: Session Expiration and Refresh Token Failures

content.content:
This fictional runbook defines incident response for the Harbor microservices system. All severity rules, role names, and examples are invented. It applies to identity, orders, payments, gateway, and notification services. Times are measured from the first actionable alert, and incident timelines use UTC.  
An alert is evidence of a symptom, not a diagnosis. The incident record must distinguish observed impact, confirmed causes, and unverified hypotheses. A responder may begin mitigation before the underlying cause is known, provided the action and its outcome are recorded.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership

content.content:
| Severity | Operational trigger | Primary acknowledgment | Status update cadence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SEV1 | Widespread sign-in or checkout failure; confirmed duplicate captures; or financial exposure that cannot be bounded | Five minutes | Every fifteen minutes |
| SEV2 | Partial service degradation sustained for ten minutes, or payment command age above fifteen minutes across multiple partitions | Ten minutes | Every thirty minutes |
| SEV3 | Limited impact with a verified workaround and no unresolved financial exposure | Four business hours | Daily while active |  
The incident commander can raise severity immediately as scope becomes clearer. A second receipt message alone is not proof of duplicate capture. A request timeout alone does not establish whether a payment committed.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership

content.content:
For SEV1, page the service primary immediately. If acknowledgment is absent at five minutes, contact the secondary rotation. Assign an incident commander by ten minutes, involving the platform duty lead if that role remains vacant.  
For SEV2, contact the secondary at twenty minutes without acknowledgment. Do not wait for that deadline when new evidence satisfies SEV1 criteria. For SEV3, assign a named role owner and a next review time in the issue tracker.  
Use the fictional role directory rather than personal contact details. Keep request correlation identifiers, affected revisions, and aggregate counts in updates; exclude credentials, bearer tokens, and customer payment payloads.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership

content.content:
The service primary diagnoses the affected component and proposes mitigation. The incident commander coordinates sequencing, severity changes, and status updates. The release operator executes an approved rollback or configuration correction and records the resulting revision.  
The payments reconciliation owner determines whether indeterminate attempts reached capture. The communications owner describes confirmed user impact without presenting hypotheses as established facts. The scribe maintains the evidence timeline and assigns unresolved questions before handoff.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership

content.content: In fictional incident `SYN-OPS-039`, a payment error alert remained unacknowledged for nine minutes. The alerting system showed successful dispatch to rotation `payments-legacy-primary`, which had no assigned responder. A retired routing rule was the confirmed cause of the delayed acknowledgment.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership
metadata.section: Example: Delayed Response to a Payment Alert

content.content: A paging-provider outage was suggested but unsupported: the dispatch log showed acceptance, and the configured destination was already incorrect. The underlying payment failure required its own investigation; the paging defect did not explain payment errors.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership
metadata.section: Example: Delayed Response to a Payment Alert

content.content:
Observe restored service for at least fifteen minutes and verify the affected user journey. Lower error rates alone are insufficient when payment outcomes remain uncertain. Keep reconciliation explicitly open with an owner and deadline, and retain SEV1 while financial exposure cannot be bounded.  
Use [Kafka backlog recovery criteria](payments-kafka-consumer-lag.md), [database timeout diagnostics](payments-database-timeout.md), or [identity Redis recovery](identity-redis-outage.md) for component-specific checks. Apply [payment idempotency rules](payments-idempotency.md) before replaying financial work. Close the incident only after impact, unresolved work, and ownership are documented.

metadata.title: Incident Severity, Escalation, and Operational Ownership

content.content:
This fictional runbook covers `notification-dispatcher` in the Harbor microservices system and incident `SYN-NOT-063`. All identifiers, policies, and outcomes are invented. The dispatcher receives order and payment events, then sends email or push notifications through a fictional delivery adapter. Delivery failure does not reverse a payment or cancel an order.  
Each logical notification has a deduplication tuple of `event_id`, channel, and `template_revision`. The dispatcher retains that tuple for thirty days and assigns one stable `delivery_id` to its delivery attempts. A legitimate resend with changed content requires an explicitly approved new template revision or event.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content:
During `SYN-NOT-063`, customers reported two payment receipt messages for one purchase. Eleven synthetic delivery records showed two adapter acceptances associated with the same logical notification. Payment ledger inspection showed one capture per corresponding purchase reference.  
The retry queue grew after the adapter intermittently returned HTTP 503 or closed connections without an acknowledgment. This was different from two independent payment requests producing separate financial operations; message count alone could not establish duplicate charging.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content:
A dispatcher release generated a new `delivery_id` for each transport retry. When the adapter accepted the first attempt but its acknowledgment was lost, the next attempt appeared to be a new delivery. Event-level deduplication prevented a second queue entry but did not stop retries within the existing entry from using new identifiers.  
Correlated acceptance records confirmed this sequence for eleven notifications. Three additional deliveries had no definitive acceptance record from their first attempt; whether they produced duplicates remains unknown pending reconciliation.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content: Duplicate Kafka events and repeated payment captures were considered. The affected records had one logical notification entry, and the checked ledger entries contained one capture. These observations did not support either hypothesis for the confirmed set.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content:
Retry connection failures, HTTP 408, HTTP 429, and HTTP 5xx responses. Stop automatic delivery for HTTP 400, 401, 403, or 422 and record the rejection reason for operator review. A 401 may require restoring adapter authorization before an approved replay.  
Allow six total attempts, including the initial send. The five retry ceilings are ten, twenty, forty, eighty, and 120 seconds, controlled by `NOTIFY_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS=10` and `NOTIFY_BACKOFF_CAP_SECONDS=120`. Draw each delay randomly between zero and its ceiling. If the adapter supplies a valid `Retry-After`, use it as the minimum wait, even when it exceeds the backoff cap.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content: An interrupted response means acceptance is unknown. Retain the same `delivery_id`; the fictional adapter deduplicates that identifier for thirty days. Do not generate a new identifier to make a retry appear fresh. After the final failed attempt, move the record to `notification.review` with its attempt history.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content: Responders restored stable delivery identifiers and paused manual replays until they checked adapter acceptance records. A controlled lost-acknowledgment exercise then produced one recipient delivery across repeated attempts. The three unresolved records remained assigned to the notification owner; they were not reported as confirmed duplicates or confirmed successes.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content: Before replaying events older than thirty days, review the expired deduplication window. Consult [payment idempotency](payments-idempotency.md) when duplicate receipts raise concerns about duplicate captures. Inbound [gateway throttling](gateway-rate-limiting.md) is separate from adapter-side 429 responses. Use the [escalation runbook](incident-escalation.md) when delays affect required customer updates.

metadata.title: Notification Retries and Duplicate Delivery Prevention

content.content:
This fictional incident report describes `SYN-ORD-114` in the Harbor microservices system. All identifiers, timings, and configuration values are synthetic. The `orders-api` service creates orders and contacts `payments-api` through a named routing profile. On 2025-06-03, a deployment introduced HTTP 500 responses for new checkout orders while order-history reads remained available.  
The new release used the same application image as the preceding release. Only the deployment configuration changed. This distinction helped responders investigate runtime settings without assuming that an application binary regression had occurred.

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content:
Forty percent of order-creation requests returned `ORD-CONFIG-500`. The affected replicas logged `PAYMENT_PROFILE_NOT_FOUND` before opening an outbound connection. Existing orders remained readable, and the process health endpoint returned HTTP 200.  
Payment service dashboards showed normal latency and no corresponding increase in incoming order requests. Clients occasionally retried checkout and received another 500 from the same replica. Requests routed to older replicas succeeded with the same synthetic test account and basket.

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content:
The deployment set `PAYMENTS_ENDPOINT_PROFILE=mesh-v3`, but the release's profile catalog contained only `mesh-v2`. The order-creation handler resolved this setting lazily on its first payment call. Basic readiness checked the process and order database, so replicas entered service before the missing profile was detected.  
Responders compared effective configuration across old and new replicas and reproduced the error using the unsupported profile. `PAYMENTS_CLIENT_TOKEN_SOURCE=workload` was correct on both generations. The confirmed problem was selecting a nonexistent route profile, rather than an expired service credential or unavailable payment backend.

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content: An expired JWT, database pool exhaustion, and a broken service route were initial hypotheses. Signature diagnostics and order database metrics were normal. Traces showed no attempted payment connection, so downstream network failure could not explain these requests. No evidence linked the deployment to the earlier payment database incident.

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content:
1. Group failures by replica and deployment revision. Compare order creation with order-history reads to establish the affected path.
2. Read the effective `PAYMENTS_ENDPOINT_PROFILE`, not only the source manifest. Compare it with the profile catalog bundled with that release.
3. Check whether a payment client span exists. Missing outbound spans plus `PAYMENT_PROFILE_NOT_FOUND` identify failure before remote execution.
4. Match the order's purchase reference with the payment ledger before advising a retry. Other failure modes may reach the payment service and lose the response.

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content:
The release operator halted the rollout and restored `PAYMENTS_ENDPOINT_PROFILE=mesh-v2`. A canary then completed order creation, payment admission, and order-history retrieval using a synthetic purchase. Responders resumed traffic only after the canary's effective configuration matched the verified profile.  
The application image remained unchanged during recovery. Error rates fell below one percent within seven minutes. Responders observed the repaired generation for fifteen minutes before completing the rollout.

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content:
The deployment checklist now requires validating named profiles before accepting traffic and exercising an order-creation transaction on the canary. A process liveness response alone is insufficient evidence that checkout dependencies are configured correctly.  
For post-admission payment delays, consult [consumer lag diagnostics](payments-kafka-consumer-lag.md). For uncertain payment outcomes after a retry, apply [idempotency rules](payments-idempotency.md). Assign release rollback and incident coordination responsibilities according to the [escalation runbook](incident-escalation.md).

metadata.title: Order Creation Failures After a Configuration Deployment

content.content:
This fictional operational record covers incident `SYN-PAY-326` in the Harbor microservices system. All technical settings and observations are invented. The synchronous `payments-api` service records payment attempts in the PostgreSQL database `payments_store`. Eight API replicas each allow twelve database connections, leaving twenty-four connections reserved within the API database role's limit of 120.  
On 2025-05-19, a receipt-enrichment release caused HTTP 504 responses during payment submission. Some clients described the result as “checkout frozen,” although the immediate failure was waiting for a database connection rather than waiting for a Kafka consumer.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content:
The API returned `PAY-DB-POOL-017` after its 750-millisecond pool-acquisition deadline. `db_pool_in_use` stayed at twelve on each affected replica, while `db_pool_waiters` rose sharply. Request latency approached the gateway timeout and successful throughput fell by sixty percent.  
Database CPU remained at thirty-five percent. Several sessions appeared as `idle in transaction`, and query execution time itself remained normal. Kafka's oldest-command age stayed below two minutes during the first ten minutes of the incident.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content:
The new receipt lookup held an open database transaction while waiting as long as twelve seconds for an external receipt response. Connections remained checked out during that network wait. At the observed arrival rate, all ninety-six API connections became occupied, leaving new requests queued until acquisition timed out.  
Responders matched connection checkout spans to receipt-call spans and reproduced the behavior with a deliberately delayed receipt response. The database was reachable; neither a slow SQL query nor the configured connection count alone explained the incident.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content: A database lock storm and excessive Kafka replay were considered. Lock-wait metrics and consumer progress did not support those explanations. The receipt service's own reason for responding slowly was not established in this investigation and remains unknown.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content:
1. Compare connection acquisition time with query execution time. `PAY-DB-POOL-017` identifies pool waiting, not necessarily SQL execution failure.
2. Count active connections across every API replica and inspect transaction age. Include rollout overlap when checking the database role's connection budget.
3. Correlate long checkouts with outbound calls and record transaction identifiers without copying payment payloads.
4. Find each timed-out request using its original idempotency key or purchase reference. A client timeout does not establish whether an earlier transaction committed.
5. If API admission is healthy but commands remain pending, use the [Kafka lag procedure](payments-kafka-consumer-lag.md) instead.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content:
Responders set `PAYMENT_RECEIPT_LOOKUP_IN_TX=false` through the existing emergency feature switch. This disabled optional receipt enrichment and restored the previously verified transaction path. Connections drained as outstanding receipt calls reached their deadlines.  
Operators did not raise every pool limit: eight pools of twenty would exceed the API role's total allowance before reserving operational headroom. They reconciled indeterminate payment attempts under the [idempotency procedure](payments-idempotency.md), retaining the original key for retries.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content:
Recovery required pool acquisition below fifty milliseconds at the ninety-fifth percentile, no growing waiter queue, and fewer than one percent payment request errors for fifteen minutes. Twenty-seven timed-out attempts were reconciled; the ledger showed one capture per purchase reference in that set.  
Release checks now include delayed receipt responses and connection-hold duration. Use the [escalation procedure](incident-escalation.md) if reconciliation cannot bound financial exposure, even after request latency returns to normal.

metadata.title: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Requests

content.content:
This fictional runbook covers duplicate-request handling in the Harbor microservices system and incident `SYN-PAY-338`. Every identifier, retention period, and outcome is invented. `payments-api` requires an `Idempotency-Key` for payment submission. The key identifies one intended operation, not one network attempt.  
Records reside in PostgreSQL alongside the payment ledger, independently of the identity service's Redis session store. Their uniqueness scope is merchant identifier, operation type, and key. A browser-generated key such as `demo-purchase-028-attempt-a` is only a synthetic example, not an authentication credential.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content:
During `SYN-PAY-338`, customers retried checkout after an HTTP 504 and later saw two captures for one purchase reference. Ledger reconciliation confirmed duplicate captures for two synthetic purchases. Other reports involved repeated receipt messages without repeated ledger captures.  
The API recorded different idempotency keys for the confirmed duplicate requests. Several same-key retries instead returned HTTP 202 because the original operation was still processing; this response alone was not a duplicate-payment failure.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content:
A client release generated a new key whenever it retried a timed-out submission. Two original requests had committed before their responses were lost. Their retries used different keys and were admitted as new operations, producing additional captures.  
The uniqueness constraint behaved as configured. It prevented duplicate execution within a key's scope but did not merge different keys merely because they shared a purchase reference. The client retry policy was the confirmed defect for the two reconciled purchases.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content: Kafka redelivery and notification duplication were considered separately. No replayed command caused the two confirmed extra captures. Two other purchase references remained under reconciliation because adapter acknowledgments were unavailable. Exposure was bounded to at most one additional capture per reference; their final financial outcomes remained unknown.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content:
- Missing key: reject with HTTP 400 and `PAY-IDEM-400` before admitting work.
- Same key and canonical payload while processing: return HTTP 202 with `PAY-IDEM-202` and `Retry-After=2`.
- Same key and payload after completion: return the stored terminal result without another capture.
- Same key with changed canonical payload: return HTTP 409 and `PAY-IDEM-409`; do not overwrite the existing record.  
Canonical payload comparison includes `amount_minor`, currency, and `purchase_ref`; transport trace identifiers are excluded. Terminal success and decline records remain for twenty-four hours after completion. Processing or uncertain records do not expire automatically while reconciliation is open. After terminal-record expiry, reusing an old key may admit new work and requires checking the durable purchase ledger first.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content:
1. Collect purchase reference, operation identifier, key, payload fingerprint, and response status without recording payment instrument details.
2. Compare keys and fingerprints across attempts. Trace a timeout through the ledger rather than assuming rollback.
3. Keep the original key and payload for retries within retention. For uncertain or expired records, pause automatic resubmission and assign the reconciliation owner.
4. Preserve the original operation identifier when handling Kafka redelivery. Commit command offsets only after durable ledger progress.  
Responders restored stable client keys and reconciled the two confirmed extra captures through the standard reversal workflow. Repeated concurrent submissions with one key then produced one financial operation in a controlled exercise.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content: Combine [database timeout diagnostics](payments-database-timeout.md) with this runbook when a client cannot determine whether submission committed. Use [consumer lag recovery](payments-kafka-consumer-lag.md) for pending commands and [notification deduplication](notifications-retry-policy.md) for repeated receipts. Apply the [escalation rules](incident-escalation.md) immediately for confirmed duplicate captures or unbounded financial exposure.

metadata.title: Duplicate Payment Requests and Idempotency Keys

content.content:
This fictional incident record describes `SYN-PAY-317` in the Harbor microservices system. Every event, identifier, and measurement is invented. `payments-api` accepts asynchronous payment requests and returns HTTP 202 after durable admission. The `payments-worker` service consumes commands from Kafka topic `payment.commands.v2`, using consumer group `payment-executors` across twelve partitions.  
On 2025-05-12, accepted payments remained pending while checkout requests continued succeeding. This runbook concerns delayed execution after admission; a successful HTTP 202 does not mean that money has been captured.

metadata.title: Kafka Consumer Lag and Delayed Payment Processing

content.content:
Consumer lag reached 18,400 records, and the oldest pending command was twenty-four minutes old. Customers saw “Payment processing” for longer than the normal two-minute target. The group repeatedly logged `PAY-CONSUMER-REBALANCE`, and partition ownership moved among three worker replicas.  
Database pool acquisition stayed below twenty milliseconds. Broker storage utilization and produce acknowledgment latency remained normal. These observations distinguished the backlog from the [database timeout incident](payments-database-timeout.md), which disrupted request handling before clients received a reliable outcome.

metadata.title: Kafka Consumer Lag and Delayed Payment Processing

content.content:
A worker performed a blocking risk-service call while processing a batch of up to 1,000 records. Its `RISK_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS=360000` exceeded `MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS=300000`. A single slow risk assessment could therefore prevent the next poll for longer than the group allowed.  
The broker removed that consumer, reassigned its partitions, and replayed commands whose offsets had not been committed. Trace timestamps showed six-minute waits immediately before each membership loss. Increasing replicas alone did not remove this blocking call.

metadata.title: Kafka Consumer Lag and Delayed Payment Processing

content.content: The reason for the risk-service delay remained unknown when this record was closed. A network interruption and an overloaded risk-service dependency were hypotheses without sufficient trace evidence. Responders did not classify either as a confirmed downstream outage. Broker capacity exhaustion was investigated but unsupported by the collected metrics.

metadata.title: Kafka Consumer Lag and Delayed Payment Processing

content.content:
1. Measure lag per partition and oldest-command age. Aggregate lag alone can hide one stalled partition.
2. Compare group membership changes with poll intervals and worker traces. Identify which processing stage holds the batch.
3. Check database checkout time and durable ledger progress before attributing every pending payment to Kafka.
4. Inspect the command's payment identifier and idempotency record before replaying it. A repeated Kafka delivery can refer to an already completed capture.

metadata.title: Kafka Consumer Lag and Delayed Payment Processing

content.content:
Responders applied the established worker profile: `RISK_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS=5000` and `MAX_POLL_RECORDS=50`. Timed-out assessments were recorded durably as deferred work before transfer to `payment.risk-retry.v1`. The worker acknowledged an original command only after the corresponding ledger state was durable.  
With poll stability restored, operators increased workers from three to six within the twelve-partition limit. They avoided resetting offsets to the topic beginning. The backlog drained in thirty-one minutes; recovery required oldest-command age below two minutes and stable membership for fifteen minutes.

metadata.title: Kafka Consumer Lag and Delayed Payment Processing

content.content:
Alert on command age as well as offset distance. Exercise a slow risk assessment during worker release checks and compare processing deadlines with the poll limit.  
Use [payment idempotency rules](payments-idempotency.md) when reconciling redelivered commands. Send delayed customer updates through the [notification retry procedure](notifications-retry-policy.md), preserving the original event identity. Follow the [escalation runbook](incident-escalation.md) if pending age exceeds fifteen minutes across multiple partitions.
